summary:
Earth analogs for Moon and Mars bases: summary
No single place on Earth matches the Moon or Mars, so NASA uses a portfolio of sites. Each one tests a different part of a mission: geology, environment, or operations such as habitat life, spacesuits, communication delay and crew dynamics.
Key sites
Devon Island, Canada (Moon + Mars): At 75°N, with sunlight similar to the Martian equator, and the 14-mile Haughton crater. Apollo astronauts trained here. It is the closest overall Mars match, and its polar setting suits lunar polar work.
Hawaiian volcanoes (Moon + Mars): HI-SEAS sits at 2,400 m on Mauna Loa and runs 4–12 month crew missions with a built-in communication delay. The volcanic ground resembles lunar and Martian soil, so resource-use hardware is tested here too.
MDRS, Utah (Mars): Founded in 2001, with 270+ crews hosted. It focuses on field science and simulated spacewalks.
Antarctica (Moon + Mars): The McMurdo Dry Valleys are the closest match to today's Martian surface. NASA also tested an inflatable lunar habitat at McMurdo for a year.
Engineered sites: CHAPEA in Houston is a 3D-printed Mars habitat whose first crew lived 378 days inside. HERA runs missions of up to 45 days, Aquarius is underwater, and lava caves mirror radiation-shelter plans.
